pages.x: In April 1876 the Bulgarians rose against Ottoman rule. The rising was crushed by irregular troops who burned villages and killed thousands. At Batak most of the village was massacred, many in the church where they had taken refuge. Reports by an American journalist shocked Europe, and in Britain Gladstone wrote a furious pamphlet, The Bulgarian Horrors.

Alexander II, who had freed Russia's serfs, came under pressure from Russians who saw themselves as the protectors of their fellow Orthodox Slavs. Serbia had fought the Ottomans in 1876 and been beaten. On 24 April 1877 Russia declared war, and Romania let its armies march through to the Danube.

On the night of 27 June the Russians crossed the Danube at Svishtov in boats and on rafts, and pushed south. A small force under General Gurko raced ahead over the Balkan mountains, and in July the Russians seized the Shipka Pass, the main road through them.

Then the advance stuck. Osman Pasha dug his army into earthworks around the town of Plevna, and threw back three great Russian and Romanian assaults, in July and September. The Russians settled down to starve him out. In December, his food gone, Osman tried to break out, was wounded, and surrendered.

All summer and autumn, Russian soldiers and Bulgarian volunteers held the Shipka Pass against the Ottoman attacks. In August, it is said, when their bullets ran out they hurled stones, and even the bodies of the dead, down on the attackers. Through the winter that followed, many froze at their posts.

With Plevna fallen, the Russians crossed the Balkan mountains in the depth of winter. Gurko took Sofia on 4 January 1878, the Ottoman armies broke, and by February the Russians were camped at San Stefano, within sight of Constantinople, while a British fleet sailed into the Sea of Marmara to warn them off.

At San Stefano, on 3 March 1878, the Ottomans signed away most of their Balkan lands. Serbia, Montenegro and Romania became fully independent, and a great new Bulgaria was created, stretching from the Danube to the Aegean. Britain and Austria-Hungary feared it would be Russia's puppet.

That summer the great powers met in Berlin under Bismarck and tore the treaty up. Big Bulgaria was split in three: a smaller Bulgaria, a self-governing Ottoman province to its south, and Macedonia, handed back to the sultan. Austria-Hungary was allowed to occupy Bosnia, and Britain took over Cyprus.

Bulgaria was free again after almost five hundred years of Ottoman rule, and every year it marks 3 March, the day of San Stefano, as its national day. But the hopes left unfulfilled in Berlin, above all for Macedonia and Bosnia, fed the Balkan Wars and, in 1914, a world war.
pts: Russia fought for the Balkan Christians
Berlin cut Bulgaria back months later
